prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

tool_items.content:
#

[![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![Pull Request Checks](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api/actions/workflows/pull-request-checks.yaml/badge.svg?branch=staging)](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api/actions/workflows/pull-request-checks.yaml) _This API is utilized by USAspending.gov to obtain all federal spending data which is open source and provided to the public as part of the DATA Act._ ![USAspending Landing Page](readme.jpg?raw=true "Readme") ## Creating a Development Environment Ensure the following dependencies are installed and working prior to continuing: ### Requirements - [`docker`](https://docs.docker.com/install/) which will handle the other application dependencies. - [`docker compose`](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) - `bash` or another Unix Shell equivalent - Bash is available on Windows as [Windows Subsystem for Linux](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install-win10) - [`git`](https://git-scm.com/downloads) - [`make`](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/) for running build/test/run targets in the `Makefile`. (Run `$ make` for a list of targets.) _**If not using Docker, you'll need to install app components on your machine:**_ > _Using Docker is recommended since it provides a clean environment. Setting up your own local environment requires some technical abilities and experience with modern software tools._ - Command line package manager - Windows' WSL bash uses `apt` - MacOS users can use [`Homebrew`](https://brew.sh/) - Linux users already know their package manager (`yum`, `apt`, `pacman`, etc.) - [`PostgreSQL`](https://www.postgresql.org/download/) version 16.x (with a dedicated `data_store_api` database) - [`OpenSearch`](https://www.elastic.co/downloads/elasticsearch) version 2.9 - `Python` version 3.10 environment - Highly recommended to use a virtual environment. There are various tools and associated instructions depending on preferences - See [Required Python Libraries](#required-python-libraries) for an example using `uv` - [`uv`](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) python package/project manager ### Cloning the Repository Now, navigate to the base file directory where you will store the USAspending repositories ```shell mkdir -p usaspending && cd usaspending git clone https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api.git cd usaspending-api ``` ### Environment Variables Choose an option between `.env` and `.envrc` that best fits your preferred workflow. Pay close attention to the values in these environment variables as usage of `localhost` vs a container's name differ between local setups. #### Create Your `.env` File (recommended) Copy the template `.env` file with local runtime environment variables defined. Change as needed for your environment. _This file is git-ignored and will not be committed by git if changed._ ```shell cp .env.template .env ``` A `.env` file is a common way to manage environment variables in a declarative file. Certain tools, like `docker compose`, will read and honor these variables. #### Create Your `.envrc` File _[direnv](https://direnv.net/) is a shell extension that automatically runs shell commands in a `.envrc` file (commonly env var `export` commands) when entering or exiting a folder with that file_ Create a `.envrc` file in the repo root, which will be ignored by git. Change credentials and ports as-needed for your local dev environment. ```shell export DATABASE_URL=postgres://usaspending:usaspender@localhost:5432/data_store_api export ES_HOSTNAME=http://localhost:9200 export BROKER_DB=postgres://usaspending:usaspender@localhost:5432/data_broker ``` If `direnv` does not pick this up after saving the file, type ```shell direnv allow ``` _Alternatively, you could skip using `direnv` and just export these variables in your shell environment._ **Just make sure your env vars declared in the shell and in `.env` match for a consistent experience inside and outside of Docker** ### Build the Docker Images _:bangbang: Re-run these commands if any python package dependencies change (in `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock`), since they are baked into the docker image at build-time._ #### usaspending-backend | usaspending-download _These images are used as the basis for running the API and download containerized setup services._ ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending build ``` #### usaspending-development _This image is used as the basis for local development including but not limited to: tests, spark jobs, linting, etc._ ```shell docker compose --profile test build ``` ### Database Setup A postgres database is required to run the app. You can run it in a `postgres` docker container (preferred), or run a PostgreSQL server on your local machine. In either case, it will be empty until data is loaded. - :warning: If running your own PostgreSQL server be sure to: 1. Have a DB named `data_store_api` 2. A superuser role (user), e.g. `ALTER ROLE <> WITH SUPERUSER;` 3. Cross-check your `.env` or `.envrc` files if used to be sure it references your DBs user, password, host, and port where needed ##### Start the Postgres DB Container _If not using your own local install..._ ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-db ``` ... will create and run a Postgres database. Use the following commands to create necessary users and set the `usaspending` user's search_path ```shell docker exec -it usaspending-db sh -c " \ psql \ -h localhost \ -p 5432 \ -U usaspending \ -d data_store_api \ -c 'CREATE USER etl_user;' \ -c 'CREATE USER readonly;' \ -c 'ALTER USER usaspending SET search_path TO public,raw,int,temp,rpt;' \ " ``` ##### Bring DB Schema Up-to-Date - To run [Django migrations](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/2.2/topics/migrations/). ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py migrate ``` - To provision the materialized views which are required by certain API endpoints. ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py matview_runner --dependencies ``` ##### Seeding and Loading Database Data _To just get essential reference data, you can run:_ - To load essential reference data (agencies, program activity codes, CFDA program data, country codes, and others). ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py load_reference_data ``` _Alternatively, to download a fully populated production snapshot of the database (full or a subset) and restore it into PostgreSQL, use the `pg_restore` tool as described here: [USAspending Database Download](https://onevoicecrm.my.site.com/usaspending/s/database-download)_ - Recreate matviews with the command documented in the previous section if this is done _**Executing individual data-loaders** to load in data is also possible, but requires more familiarity with those ad-hoc scripts and commands, and also requires an external data source (Data Broker DB, or external file, etc.) from which to load the data._ - For details on loading reference data, Data Accountability Broker Submissions, and current USAspending data into the API, see [loading_data.md](loading_data.md). - For details on how our data loaders modify incoming data, see [data_reformatting.md](data_reformatting.md). ### OpenSearch Setup Some API endpoints reach into OpenSearch for data. ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-es ``` ... will create and start a single-node OpenSearch cluster as a docker container with data persisted to a docker volume. - The cluster should be reachable via at http://localhost:9200 ("You Know, for Search"). - Optionally, to see log output, use `docker compose logs usaspending-es` (these logs are stored by docker even if you don't use this). While not required, it is highly recommended to also create the OpenSearch Dashboards docker container for querying the OpenSearch cluster. ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-kibana-es ``` #### Generate Elasticsearch Indexes The following will generate the indexes: ```shell CURR_DATE=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S') docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-transactions" --load-type transaction docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-awards" --load-type award docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-recipients" --load-type recipient docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-subaward" --load-type subaward ``` ### Observability/Tracing Setup The project uses grafana, tempo, and opentelemetry for observability. This enables developers to trace functionality across multiple services resulting in better visibility of issues. There are two options for using the observability framework in the local development setup. You can log traces to the console by setting the `TOGGLE_OTEL_CONSOLE_LOGGING` environmental variable to `True` for the `usaspending-api` container. Alternatively you can run the `otel-collector`, `tempo`, and `grafana` containers to more fully replicate the production observability framework. These containers are part of the `tracing` profile and can be brought up with: ```shell docker compose --profile tracing up -d ``` When using these containers the `TOGGLE_OTEL_CONSOLE_LOGGING` must be set to `False` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` must be set to `http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces` ### Install python version with uv Install the currently supported python version with uv. This is useful for access to a python shell outside a container. However, it is recommended to use the docker compose containerized services for interaction with the API, spark, and tests. ```shell uv python install 3.10.12 ``` #### Sync uv project with lockfile Setup uv project and check version info: ```shell make local-dev-setup ``` ## Running the API Run the following to bring up the Django app for the RESTful API: ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up usaspending-api ``` You can update environment variables in `settings.py` (buckets, elasticsearch, local paths) and they will be mounted and used when you run this. The application will now be available at `http://localhost:8000`. _**NOTE**: if the code was run outside of Docker then compiled Python files will potentially trip up the docker environment. A useful command to run for clearing out the files on your host is:_ ```shell find . | grep -E "(__pycache__|\.pyc|\.pyo$)" | xargs rm -rf ``` #### Using the API In your local development environment, available API endpoints may be found at `http://localhost:8000/docs/endpoints`. Deployed production API endpoints and docs are found by following links here: `https://api.usaspending.gov`. ## Running Tests ### Test Setup 1. Build the base `usaspending-development` Docker image (the test container is based on this Docker image). In the parent **usaspending-api** directory run: ```shell docker build -t usaspending-development -f development.Dockerfile . ``` 2. Start the Spark containers for the Spark related tests ```shell docker compose --profile spark up -d ``` 3. To run all USAspending tests in the docker services run ```shell docker compose run --rm -e BROKER_DB='' usaspending-test ``` _**NOTE**: If an env var named `BROKER_DB` is set, Broker Integration tests will attempt to be run as well. If doing so, Broker dependencies must be met (see below) or ALL tests will fail hard. Running the above command with `-e BROKER_DB=''` is a precaution to keep them excluded, unless you really want them (see below if so)._ To run tests locally and not in the docker services, you need: 1. **Postgres**: A running PostgreSQL database server _(See [Database Setup above](#database-setup))_ 1. **OpenSearch**: A running OpenSearch cluster _(See [OpenSearch Setup above](#opensearch-setup))_ 1. **Environment Variables**: Tell python where to connect to the various data stores _(See [Environment Variables](#environment-variables))_ 1. **Install python version with uv**: python is installed with uv _(See below)_ 1. **Sync uv project**: uv project is synced with lockfile _(See below)_ _**NOTE**: Running test locally might require you to run `export OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY=YES`. As discussed [here](https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/38560), there is an issue than can cause some of the Spark tests to fail without this environment variable set._ ### Including Broker Integration Tests Some automated integration tests run against a [Broker](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/data-act-broker-backend) database. If certain dependencies to run such integration tests are not satisfied, those tests will bail out and be marked as _Skipped_. (You can see messages about those skipped tests by adding the `-rs` flag to pytest, like: `pytest -rs`) To satisfy these dependencies and include execution of these tests, do the following: 1. Ensure the `Broker` source code is checked out alongside this repo at `../data-act-broker-backend` 1. Ensure you have [`Docker`](https://docs.docker.com/install/) installed and running on your machine 1. Ensure you have built the `Broker` backend Docker image by running: ```shell docker build -t dataact-broker-backend ../data-act-broker-backend ``` 1. Ensure you have the `BROKER_DB` environment variable set, and it points to what will be a live PostgreSQL server (no database required) at the time tests are run. 1. _WARNING: If this is set at all, then ALL above dependencies must be met or ALL tests will fail (Django will try this connection on ALL tests' run)_ 1. This DB could be one you always have running in a local Postgres instance, or one you spin up in a Docker container just before tests are run 1. If invoking `pytest` within a docker container (e.g. using the `usaspending-test` container), you _must_ mount the host's docker socket. This is declared already in the `docker-compose.yml` file services, but would be done manually with: `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` _**NOTE**: Broker source code should be re-fetched and image rebuilt to ensure latest integration is tested_ Re-running the test suite using `pytest -rs` with these dependencies satisfied should yield no more skips of the broker integration tests. **Example Test Invocations of _Just a Few_ Broker Integration Tests:** (_i.e. using `-k`_) _From within a container_ _**NOTE**: `BROKER_DB` is set in the `docker-compose.yml` file (and could pick up `.env` values, if set)_ ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-test pytest --capture=no --verbose --tb=auto --no-cov --log-cli-level=INFO -k test_broker_integration ``` _From Developer Desktop_ _**NOTE**: `BROKER_DB` is set in the `.envrc` file and available in the shell_ ```shell pytest --capture=no --verbose --tb=auto --no-cov --log-cli-level=INFO -k test_broker_integration ``` ## Contributing To submit fixes or enhancements, or to suggest changes, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: USAspending.gov
Description: USAspending.gov is the official source for spending data for the U.S. Government. Its mission is to show the American public what the federal government spends every year and how it spends the money. You can follow the money from the Congressional appropriations to the federal agencies and down to local communities and businesses.
URL: https://usaspending.gov/

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# USAspending.gov: dataset research and preservation report

**Research date: October 9, 2026**

## Executive assessment

Your title, URL, and description are substantially accurate. Treasury describes USAspending.gov as the federal government’s official source for spending data and uses essentially the mission statement you supplied. However, two qualifications are important:

1. **USAspending.gov is a data platform and collection of related datasets—not one flat dataset.** It combines agency financial-account data, federal award transactions, recipient information, subawards, reference data, and derived summaries.
2. **“Follow the money” describes its purpose, not a guarantee of complete end-to-end traceability.** Some spending is excluded, some agencies are outside reporting requirements, some awards cannot be linked to financial accounts, and subaward information does not consistently identify every ultimate beneficiary.

**Bottom line:** USAspending.gov is a high-value national transparency resource worth preserving. Its official status establishes provenance, but does not make every record complete, accurate, comparable, or suitable for every analysis. [1–4]

### Suggested catalog description

> USAspending.gov is the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s official public platform for federal spending transparency. Maintained by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, it integrates agency financial-account information with federal contracts, grants, loans, direct payments, other financial assistance, recipient information, and reported first-tier subawards. It provides searchable records, visualizations, bulk downloads, and a public API. Coverage, reporting frequency, data quality, and available fields vary by source system and historical period.

---

## 1. Identity, publisher, and institutional responsibility

| Attribute | Findings |
|---|---|
| Official title | USAspending.gov |
| Main URL | https://www.usaspending.gov/ |
| Publisher/operator | U.S. Department of the Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service |
| Policy and standards partners | Treasury and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) |
| Original data producers | Reporting federal agencies; prime recipients reporting subawards and certain compensation information; governmentwide source-system operators |
| Resource type | Continuously updated administrative-data platform |
| Subject coverage | Federal budget execution, financial accounts, procurement, financial assistance, recipients, and subawards |
| Geographic coverage | United States, territories, and foreign locations where covered awards are reported |
| Public access | Free website, downloads, and API; API documentation says endpoints do not currently require authorization |
| Principal monetary concepts | Budgetary resources, obligations, outlays, and award-specific amounts |
| Historical coverage | Varies by data product; see Section 4 |

Treasury operates the publication infrastructure, but **responsibility for the underlying records is distributed**:

- Agencies produce and submit financial and award information.
- GSA operates important upstream award and entity systems.
- Prime recipients supply reported subaward information.
- Treasury integrates, validates, transforms, and publishes the data.
- OMB establishes governmentwide reporting policy.
- GAO and agency inspectors general provide external oversight.

For cataloging, Treasury/Bureau of the Fiscal Service should be identified as publisher, while source agencies and systems should be recorded as provenance—not omitted because the records appear on a single website. [1–4]

---

## 2. Legal authority and mandate

### Foundational statutes

**Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006—FFATA, Public Law 109-282**

Signed September 26, 2006, FFATA required a publicly accessible, searchable federal award database. Its original reporting framework covered contracts, grants, loans, and other financial assistance above a statutory threshold of $25,000. OMB originally had responsibility for creating the website. **That historical threshold should not be treated as a universal current threshold for every data stream.** [1, 4]

**2008 FFATA amendment—Government Funding Transparency Act**

The amendment expanded transparency requirements, including first-tier subrecipient reporting and certain executive-compensation disclosures. USAspending’s history describes subrecipient requirements applying to awards made beginning October 1, 2010. [1]

**Digital Accountability and Transparency Act of 2014—DATA Act, Public Law 113-101**

Signed May 9, 2014, the DATA Act expanded the award-transparency framework to include agency expenditures and connections between financial accounts, programs, and awards. It also required governmentwide data standards and measures to improve reporting quality.

Its principal objectives include:

- Disclosing direct agency expenditures.
- Linking financial and award information.
- Establishing consistent, searchable financial-data standards.
- Simplifying reporting and reducing compliance costs.
- Improving agency accountability for data quality.

CRS describes the DATA Act as transferring USAspending responsibility from OMB to Treasury. FFATA and its amendments are associated with **31 U.S.C. § 6101 note**. [1, 4]

### Operational rules and standards

The statutes are implemented through additional instruments:

- **Treasury Financial Manual, Volume I, Part 2, Chapter 6000:** agency reporting requirements, submission processes, and senior accountable official responsibilities.
- **OMB guidance**, including M-20-21 on pandemic-related transparency and expanded monthly reporting, M-21-20 on American Rescue Plan implementation, and M-22-02 on financial-assistance transparency.
- **2 CFR Part 170:** financial-assistance subaward and executive-compensation reporting requirements.
- Procurement reporting rules and guidance governing upstream contract records.
- **Governmentwide Spending Data Model (GSDM):** technical definitions, submission specifications, interfaces, and validation rules. [2, 5]

**Preservation implication:** preserve the rules and standards alongside the data. A record’s meaning depends partly on the reporting obligations and schema in effect when it was created.

---

## 3. History and development

| Period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| Before USAspending | Federal spending information existed across separate procurement, assistance, financial, and statistical systems. CRS identifies Census’s *Federal Aid to States* and *Consolidated Federal Funds Report* as important earlier publications. They are historical complements, not automatically interchangeable series. |
| 2006 | FFATA established the public award-transparency mandate. |
| 2007 | The original USAspending.gov website launched. |
| 2008–2010 | Expanded subaward and compensation reporting requirements were introduced. |
| 2009 onward | Recovery Act reporting added another major transparency and oversight context. |
| 2014 | DATA Act expanded the scope from awards toward financial-account-to-award transparency and common standards. |
| April 2016 | Treasury first published the DATA Act Information Model Schema, or DAIMS. |
| 2017 | DATA Act implementation and an expanded website introduced a broader financial-account perspective. |
| June 2020 reporting period | Agencies with COVID-19 relief funding moved to monthly financial reporting, with additional emergency-funding and award-outlay requirements. |
| FY2022 onward | Reporting agencies were required to submit monthly financial data, including award-level outlays. |
| April 2022 | The government transitioned from DUNS to the SAM.gov Unique Entity ID as its primary entity identifier. |
| November 2023 | DAIMS was renamed the Governmentwide Spending Data Model, reflecting requirements beyond the original DATA Act. |
| March 2025 | FSRS subaward reporting functions moved to SAM.gov, with additional validation controls. |
| 2026 | Treasury’s schema history lists GSDM 1.2.1, released May 1, 2026, with implementation dates varying by change. |

The major historical change is **not merely a redesigned website**: USAspending evolved from an award database into an integration system connecting financial accounts and awards. Consequently, long-term trend analysis must account for changes in scope, definitions, identifiers, reporting frequency, and completeness. [1, 3–6, 10]

---

## 4. Coverage: what is included, and how far back it goes

### Principal data domains

**Agency financial data**

These describe both award and non-award spending, including:

- Budgetary resources.
- Obligations and outlays.
- Federal accounts and Treasury Account Symbols.
- Program activities.
- Object classes.
- Disaster Emergency Fund Codes.

**Prime award information**

Covered categories include:

- Contracts and related procurement records.
- Grants and cooperative agreements.
- Direct loans and loan guarantees.
- Direct payments.
- Other financial assistance.

Fields vary by award type.

**Subaward information**

Reported first-tier subcontracts and subgrants connect prime recipients to other entities carrying out federally funded work. These are not a complete transaction ledger through every successive tier.

**Recipient and reference information**

Examples include recipient names and identifiers, parent relationships, locations, agency classifications, assistance listings, industry and product/service classifications, and Census-derived geographic context. Treasury’s source overview describes more than 400 data elements across the platform. [3]

### Historical availability differs by product

| Product | Documented start |
|---|---|
| Earliest award data available through Custom Award Data Download | FY2001 |
| Advanced Search award data | FY2008 |
| DATA Act agency financial-system data | FY2017, second quarter—January 1, 2017 |
| Comprehensive monthly award-outlay reporting requirement | FY2022 |

The FY2001 statement **does not mean that every award type, subaward series, or field is complete from FY2001**. Treasury explicitly warns that reporting requirements change over time and that more recent fiscal years generally have higher-quality information. [3]

### Geographic interpretation

Records may describe:

- Recipient headquarters or registered location.
- Primary place of performance.
- State, county, city, ZIP code, congressional district, or country.

**Recipient location and place of performance answer different questions.** Neither necessarily identifies all communities benefiting from an award. A headquarters address can concentrate apparent spending in one location even when work occurs elsewhere.

---

## 5. Data sources and production workflow

USAspending’s financial-to-award model is commonly described through Files A–F.

| Component | Main content | Principal source |
|---|---|---|
| **File A** | Account balances, budgetary resources, obligations, outlays | Agency financial reporting; may be generated using GTAS data |
| **File B** | Financial-account breakdown by program activity and object class | Agency financial systems |
| **File C** | Financial-account breakdown by award | Agency financial systems |
| **File D1** | Procurement award and awardee attributes | Governmentwide procurement reporting, identified in documentation as FPDS |
| **File D2** | Financial-assistance award and awardee attributes | Financial Assistance Broker Submission—FABS |
| **File E** | Additional awardee attributes, including qualifying executive compensation | SAM.gov |
| **File F** | Subaward attributes | Prime-recipient reporting, now through SAM.gov; historically FSRS |

Other supporting sources include:

- **GTAS:** Governmentwide Treasury Account Symbol Adjusted Trial Balance System.
- Assistance-listing information.
- Agency and account reference tables.
- Geographic and demographic reference data.

Agencies submit financial files through Treasury’s **DATA Act Broker**. The process applies validation rules, supports verification/certification, and publishes accepted submissions. Treasury also extracts information from governmentwide systems and performs integration and transformations for USAspending. [2, 3]

### A critical linkage limitation

Complete award information depends on matching financial-system records with governmentwide award-system records through a common award identifier.

An **unlinked financial-system award** may lack recipient, location, industry, competition, or assistance-listing details.

An **unlinked award-system record** may lack Treasury account, program activity, object class, emergency-funding code, or outlay information.

Thus, a missing outlay is not automatically a zero, and a missing recipient is not automatically evidence of an undisclosed recipient. [3]

---

## 6. Update frequency, lag, and revisions

There is **no single update frequency** for the entire platform.

| Data stream | Documented reporting/publication pattern |
|---|---|
| Agency financial Files A–C | Monthly for reporting agencies since FY2022; published after agency verification, generally within 24 hours |
| Contract records | Treasury documentation describes new records arriving approximately two days after upstream submission |
| Financial assistance | Documentation describes at least twice-monthly reporting for most assistance, with monthly reporting described for loans |
| Executive compensation | Extracted daily from SAM.gov |
| Reportable subawards | Due by the end of the month following the month of the subaward, followed by system-ingestion lag |
| Defense-related contract records | Documentation identifies a 90-day delay for DOD and Army Corps of Engineers contract information |

Reporting deadlines, upstream entry dates, ingestion dates, and website publication dates are different events.

Historical data can also be corrected or republished. **A download made today may differ from a download of the same fiscal year made earlier.** The Agency Submission Statistics page explicitly tracks published/certified and republished/recertified submissions. [2, 3, 7]

---

## 7. Access, formats, software, and documentation

### Available access routes

- **Website search and profiles:** awards, agencies, recipients, states, and federal accounts.
- **Spending Explorer:** broader financial spending views.
- **Custom Award Data Download:** filtered award extracts.
- **Custom Account Data Download:** financial-account extracts.
- **Award Data Archive:** pregenerated award files.
- **Search-result and individual-award downloads.**
- **Public API:** programmatic access.
- **Database Download:** full or subset production database snapshots. [3, 4, 8, 9]

### Formats and technical architecture

For analysis and preservation, the principal representations include:

- Tabular downloads, notably CSV.
- API responses, principally JSON.
- PostgreSQL database snapshots restored using `pg_restore`.
- Documentation in web pages, PDFs, spreadsheets, and versioned schema packages.

The current API repository README lists a development stack including **Python/Django, PostgreSQL 16.x, OpenSearch 2.9, and Docker**. These are documented development requirements, not a guarantee about every production component.

Some API endpoints depend on search indexes and materialized views. Therefore, restoring database tables alone may not reproduce the live website or every API behavior. [9]

### Documentation to retain

- USAspending *About the Data*.
- Source-system descriptions.
- Analyst’s Guide to Federal Spending Data.
- API endpoint documentation.
- Download dictionaries and field definitions.
- GSDM Reporting Submission Specification.
- GSDM Interface Definition Document.
- Validation rules, architecture documents, examples, and historical schema releases.
- Software transformation and data-loading documentation.

**Important:** GSDM submission fields, download columns, API fields, and database columns are related but not necessarily identical. Preserve their mappings.

---

## 8. Interpretation hazards for data scientists

### Monetary concepts are not interchangeable

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Budget authority/appropriation | Legal authority to incur obligations |
| Budgetary resources | Resources available for obligation, potentially including balances and other sources—not simply new appropriations |
| Obligation | A binding commitment that will result in payment immediately or later |
| Outlay | Payment liquidating an obligation |
| Contract ceiling/potential value | Potential contract value, not necessarily obligated or paid |
| Loan face value | Principal or guaranteed amount, not equivalent to federal subsidy cost |

A report stating that a recipient “received” money should specify whether it means **obligations, outlays, loan principal, or another measure**.

### Practical safeguards

1. **Choose a record level before aggregating.** Award summaries, transactions, financial-account rows, and subawards have different units of observation.
2. **Use transaction action dates for period-specific obligation analysis.** Search results can include awards whose activity spans a selected period, while lifetime award totals answer a different question.
3. **Retain negative obligations.** Deobligations and adjustments can be legitimate.
4. **Do not sum cumulative monthly financial balances as though they were independent flows.** Check field definitions before calculating monthly or annual totals.
5. **Do not add prime and subaward amounts together as total federal spending.** Subawards generally redistribute money already represented by prime awards.
6. **Do not repeatedly sum award totals after one-to-many joins.** Account, transaction, and subaward relationships can multiply rows.
7. **Keep identifiers as text.** Leading zeros and composite identifiers matter.
8. **Use entity identifiers and documented award keys—not names alone—for matching.** Preserve both historical DUNS and UEI fields where available.
9. **Document geographic boundary vintages.** Congressional districts and classifications change.
10. **Distinguish missing, inapplicable, withheld, and zero values.**
11. **Treat dollars as nominal unless you explicitly apply an inflation adjustment.**
12. **Do not infer policy outcomes or misconduct from spending records alone.** Those claims require additional evidence.

These safeguards follow from the platform’s mixed financial concepts, historical changes, and relational structure. [2–4, 6, 9]

---

## 9. Completeness, exclusions, and independent quality evidence

### Deliberate or structural exclusions

Treasury’s documentation identifies exclusions or limitations involving:

- Personally identifiable information.
- National-security-sensitive information.
- Proprietary recipient information or documents.
- Tax expenditures, including Economic Impact Payments issued through the tax system.
- Agencies and branches outside applicable reporting requirements.
- Awards below applicable reporting thresholds.
- Incomplete account-to-award linkage.

Individual assistance beneficiaries are generally not exposed as named recipients; aggregate reporting protects privacy.

Non-award spending may appear in financial-account data without a corresponding recipient-level award record. USAspending therefore should not be described as a complete public list of every federal payment. [3]

### Independent findings

**GAO-24-106214, published November 7, 2023**

For FY2022, GAO identified **49 nonreporting agencies among 152 agencies examined**. Twenty-five were executive-branch agencies accounting for more than $5 billion in net outlays. GAO cautioned that some nonreporting agencies might not be legally required to report.

GAO also identified:

- Differences between USAspending COVID-19 obligations and other public financial reports.
- More than $40 billion in other transaction agreements not reported in its review.
- Unclear responsibility for determining the complete population of required reporting agencies. [11]

**GAO-24-106237, published November 16, 2023**

GAO documented grant-subaward problems, including incomplete, late, inaccurate, and duplicative reporting.

There has since been progress: GAO’s recommendation-status page records implementation of additional guidance, Treasury disclosures, and SAM.gov automated validation controls in 2024–2025. **Those improvements should not be assumed to have retrospectively repaired all historical records.** [10]

**GAO-25-107469**

GAO found weaknesses in procurement data-quality certification and verification. Of 70 agencies reporting FY2023 procurement information, 36 confirmed completing the relevant data-quality reports. The agencies not confirming completion represented a relatively small share of total obligations, but the finding remains relevant to uneven upstream assurance. [12]

**GAO-26-107466**

This broader interoperability review examined nine federal award/payment-eligibility data sources and identified obstacles involving dictionaries, validation rules, and cross-system consistency. It reinforces the need for explicit metadata and validation when linking federal administrative sources; it is not an error-rate estimate for all USAspending records. [13]

**Quality conclusion:** suitability must be evaluated by agency, period, award type, field, and research question. A single platform-wide label such as “accurate” or “unreliable” is inadequate.

---

## 10. Typical users and public benefits

The following are well-supported user communities and use cases, rather than a measured demographic breakdown of website visitors.

| Community | Typical use | Public benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Congress and legislative staff | District/state funding analysis and oversight | More informed appropriations and accountability |
| GAO, inspectors general, agency analysts | Reconciliation, compliance, anomaly identification | Better financial controls and audit targeting |
| Journalists and watchdog organizations | Investigating recipients, procurement, and spending changes | Public scrutiny of government decisions |
| State, local, territorial, and tribal governments | Tracking awards and federal funding exposure | Planning and coordination |
| Researchers and data scientists | Studying procurement markets, geographic allocation, and emergency spending | Reproducible policy research |
| Businesses and nonprofits | Examining prior awards, recipients, and program activity | Understanding federal funding markets |
| Librarians, educators, and residents | Reference assistance and civic learning | Accessible government financial information |
| Policy activists | Monitoring distribution, implementation, and reporting gaps | Evidence-based advocacy |

Its public value lies in **centralizing information that would otherwise be fragmented**, providing common identifiers and classifications, and allowing independent reuse rather than restricting users to government-authored summaries.

It supports fraud-risk and anomaly research, but an anomaly is not proof of fraud. It supports equity analysis, but award geography alone does not establish who ultimately benefited. [1, 3, 4]

---

## 11. Licensing, reuse, and privacy

Treasury states that USAspending data may be copied, adapted, redistributed, and used for commercial or noncommercial purposes, **subject to the site’s Dun & Bradstreet data-use limitation**. Treasury separately states that public repository code is available under **CC0**. [1, 14]

### Consequences for librarians and preservationists

- Do **not** assign an unconditional CC0 license to the entire data collection merely because the software uses CC0.
- Preserve the publisher’s general reuse statement and the third-party notice.
- Historical DUNS-associated business information requires particular attention.
- Review the applicable D&B notice before bulk redistribution or commercial reuse.
- Separate rights metadata for software, government-origin data, and third-party fields.

The government’s April 2022 transition to UEI does not, by itself, remove legal considerations attached to historical D&B-derived information.

Privacy protections also constrain analytical use: aggregated individual-benefit records should not be interpreted as identifying named people. Combining public sources can create additional privacy risks even when each source is lawful to access. [3, 6, 14]

---

## 12. Preservation assessment and recommended strategy

### Why preservation is warranted

USAspending has enduring value as evidence of:

- Government resource allocation.
- Federal relationships with companies, nonprofits, and governments.
- Emergency and disaster response.
- Procurement-market structure.
- Geographic distribution of federal commitments.
- Changes in transparency policy and reporting compliance.

It also records **what government publicly reported at a particular time**, which can differ from later corrected data.

### Principal preservation risks

- Historical records can be revised.
- Download products may be regenerated.
- API schemas and behavior can change.
- Upstream systems migrate.
- Entity identifiers and classifications change.
- A web crawl may capture only the interface, not underlying data.
- Database recovery may depend on schema versions, indexes, and software.
- Third-party rights may constrain redistribution.

**An “Award Data Archive” is not, by its name alone, evidence of immutable historical snapshots.** I did not verify a public commitment to retain every past database state, a complete deletion/change log, or a permanent archive of every generated extract.

### Recommended preservation package

Preserve, where feasible:

1. **Dated database snapshots**, plus manageable CSV exports for long-term portability.
2. **Prime transactions, award summaries, financial-account data, and subawards as distinct products.**
3. **Schemas, dictionaries, code lists, and field mappings.**
4. **Historical GSDM/DAIMS packages and validation rules.**
5. **API documentation and representative request/response examples.**
6. **Software repositories at fixed commit hashes**, with dependency files.
7. **Agency submission statistics and quality disclosures.**
8. **Licensing and third-party notices.**
9. **Release notes and source-system migration documentation.**
10. **Independent audit reports relevant to each collection period.**

Record acquisition time, source URL, filters, fiscal periods, row counts, file sizes, checksums, schema version, software commit, and retrieval failures.

**Suggested acquisition schedule—not an official requirement:** monthly snapshots after reporting deadlines, a post-year-end snapshot, and later reconciliation snapshots to capture revisions. Maintain multiple independently checked copies and periodically test database restoration.

---

## 13. Cataloging, citation, and reproducibility

### Recommended catalog fields

Include:

- Publisher and contributing agencies.
- Data-product title—not just the platform name.
- Version/snapshot or extraction date.
- Temporal and geographic coverage.
- Record level and monetary measure.
- Source systems.
- Schema and dictionary versions.
- Update frequency and reporting lag.
- Known exclusions and quality limitations.
- Rights and third-party restrictions.
- File formats and technical requirements.

# USAspending.gov dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**

## Overall finding

**The evidence points more strongly to operational and data-quality risks than to imminent removal of USAspending.gov.** Its explicit statutory mandate, continued reporting infrastructure, and substantial government and public use provide protection. However, planned Bureau of the Fiscal Service staffing reductions, leadership turnover, and pending grant-reporting changes warrant monitoring.

This assessment applies to **USAspending.gov as a governmentwide publication platform**, not to whether every agency or recipient submits every record correctly. Individual reporting failures can coexist with continued platform publication.

**Evidence limitations:** I could not complete a current agency-by-agency submission audit or download-and-compare historical files. Direct requests to the award archive and an API update-status endpoint timed out. Those tool failures are **not evidence that the service or data have been removed**. “No Known Issue” below means no qualifying problem was established—not that availability or timeliness has been exhaustively verified.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue:** Treasury continues to document historical award and financial-account access through searches and downloads. Documented coverage extends to FY2001 for some custom award downloads, FY2008 for Advanced Search, and FY2017 Q2 for DATA Act financial-account data. The [Award Data Archive](https://www.usaspending.gov/download_center/award_data_archive) remains indexed as an official access route. See also [About the Data](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/about-the-data-download.pdf).
- **Moderate Risk:** Historical records can be corrected and republished. The [Agency Submission Statistics methodology](https://www.usaspending.gov/submission-statistics/data-sources) explicitly describes publication, certification, and update histories. This establishes **mutability**, but not removal of historical data elements.
- **High Risk / Gone:** I found no substantiated evidence that USAspending has removed historical-year files or discontinued all pre-current-year access.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

No qualifying historical-file or historical-field removal was established. Routine corrections do not, by themselves, meet the rubric’s removal criteria.

**Qualification:** This is not an “unaltered archive” finding. USAspending does not necessarily preserve every previously published database state for public retrieval. A researcher may still lose the ability to reproduce an earlier result unless the original extract was saved.

**Confidence: Medium.**

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue:** Treasury’s [monthly reporting requirements](https://tfx.treasury.gov/monthly-reporting-requirements) and [Treasury Financial Manual reporting chapter](https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov) continue to prescribe submissions and publication. The [Governmentwide Spending Data Model](https://tfx.treasury.gov/data-transparency/gsdm) remains maintained, currently identifying version 1.2.1.
- **Moderate Risk:** Planned staffing reductions create a plausible risk of future delays, but I did not establish a recent platform-wide missed publication cycle.
- **High Risk:** Treasury acknowledges late and incomplete **individual subaward reporting** in [About the Data](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/about-the-data-download.pdf). That is important, but does not establish that Treasury skipped a governmentwide publication cycle or missed a platform-wide statutory deadline.
- **Gone:** No termination announcement was found.

### ICR qualification

USAspending integrates multiple administrative reporting streams; it is not one survey governed by one ICR. An ICR with “USAspending” in its title may cover **website feedback**, not spending-data collection. For example, [OMB control number 1530-0023](https://omb.report/omb/1530-0023) covers qualitative service feedback and lists an expiration of April 30, 2027. That does **not** prove that every upstream award-reporting collection has an active clearance.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Continued reporting and publication are documented, and no qualifying current platform-wide delay, skipped cycle, or collection termination was established.

**Qualification:** Current on-time performance across all agencies remains unverified. This is the least certain “No Known Issue” rating.

**Confidence: Low–Medium.**

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue:** The March 2025 migration of subaward reporting from FSRS to SAM.gov introduced additional controls intended to prevent duplicate subaward records. Treasury documents these improvements in [About the Data](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/about-the-data-download.pdf); [SAM.gov](https://sam.gov/fsrs) confirms the migration and continued public APIs.
- **Moderate Risk:** Fiscal Service’s staffing-reduction plan creates a plausible risk to validation, technical maintenance, agency assistance, and correction of reporting problems. USAspending also depends on reporting capacity across many agencies and recipients.
- **High Risk:** Treasury documents missing, duplicated, inconsistent, and late subaward records. [GAO-24-106237](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106237) independently identified these problems. However, longstanding defects are not sufficient evidence of a **new reduction** in granularity, timeliness, or frequency since January 2025.
- **Gone:** Collection and publication have not been shown to have terminated.

There is also evidence of continuing analytical usefulness: [GAO-26-108615](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-108615/index.html) used USAspending to examine DOGE savings claims and judged the relevant data sufficiently reliable **for that particular purpose**.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

There is a concrete emerging capacity risk, superimposed on established reporting weaknesses. I did not find sufficient evidence of an implemented platform-wide reduction to justify **High Risk** under this rubric.

**Important distinction:** This rating concerns deterioration risk. It is not a certification that existing records are uniformly accurate.

**Confidence: Medium.**

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue:** USAspending’s legal foundation is explicit:
  - Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006, **Public Law 109-282**.
  - Digital Accountability and Transparency Act of 2014, **Public Law 113-101**.
  - Implementing requirements in [2 CFR Part 170](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/subtitle-A/chapter-I/part-170), including §170.200’s express requirement to publish covered award information on USAspending.gov.
  - Operational specifications in the [Treasury Financial Manual](https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov).
- **Moderate Risk:** The “not explicitly required by statute” condition does not fit this platform.
- **High Risk:** SAM.gov, procurement systems, agency reports, and Treasury Fiscal Data provide overlapping information, but none alone replaces USAspending’s integrated public account-and-award publication function. Programmatic and oversight use is well established, including GAO’s recent use.
- **Gone:** Not applicable under the rubric.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

The collection and public-transparency function have an explicit statutory foundation and defined reporting requirements. This is the strongest protective factor.

The mandate does **not** guarantee uninterrupted hosting, perfect compliance, or preservation of every historical version.

**Confidence: High.**

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Scope:** Bureau of the Fiscal Service, the operating bureau—not Treasury’s entire workforce, which includes much larger organizations such as IRS.

### Evidence by risk level

- **Moderate Risk:** Treasury’s [FY2026 Fiscal Service Congressional Justification](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/266/13.-Fiscal-FY-2026-CJ.pdf) plans:
  - Appropriated FTE decreasing from **1,424 to 1,109**: a net reduction of **315 FTE, approximately 22.1%**.
  - Total bureau FTE decreasing from **1,746 to 1,431**, approximately **18.0%**.
  - Reductions through deferred resignation, early retirement, planned reductions in force, and attrition.

  Both percentage measures fall within the rubric’s **10–39%** moderate band, **if realized**.
- **No Known Issue—funding counterevidence:** The same request keeps Salaries and Expenses at **$391.1 million**, flat with the FY2025 operating plan. Total budgetary resources are approximately flat. It reallocates savings toward payment integrity rather than proposing a 20% bureau-wide funding cut. The [Budget in Brief](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/266/12.-Fiscal-FY-2026-BIB.pdf) continues to describe USAspending within accounting and reporting operations.
- **Leadership:** Fiscal Service’s [leadership page](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/about-us) says Joseph Gioeli became acting commissioner on April 30, 2026. The [Association of Government Accountants biography](https://aga.digitellinc.com/b/sp/tim-gribben-1661) identifies predecessor Tim Gribben’s departure as retirement. This is turnover, but not evidence of a forced removal of the USAspending leadership team.
- **High Risk / Gone:** I did not verify a 40% bureau staffing loss, 1,000 bureau departures, a 20% bureau budget cut, forced removal of USAspending leadership, or elimination of its staff or funding.

### Staffing-tracker findings

The requested [USAJobs tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) states that collection would stop December 31, 2025. It also warns that **job postings are not actual hires**. It therefore cannot establish current bureau headcount or the percentage of USAspending staff lost.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk — provisional**

The official workforce plan supports a substantial capacity concern in the moderate range. **It is a budget projection, not a verified count of completed departures**, and I found no USAspending-team-specific staffing series.

Strictly applying the rubric only to confirmed realized losses would leave this category unresolved. Moderate Risk is the most appropriate precautionary selection, with that limitation explicit.

**Confidence: Medium for the plan; Low for realized team-level effects.**

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

- **Moderate Risk:** OMB’s May 29, 2026 [proposed rule, “Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance”](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance), proposes changes directly relevant to USAspending’s upstream data:
  - Stronger agency and pass-through-entity oversight of subaward reporting.
  - Tracking transfers to affiliates, subsidiaries, and related organizations as subawards where applicable.
  - Replacing obsolete FSRS references with SAM.gov.
  
  The proposal expressly discusses GAO’s findings about incomplete and inaccurate USAspending subaward data. I did not verify a final rule implementing these provisions.
- **No Known Issue—counterevidence:** Much of the proposal aims to **improve**, rather than suppress, transparency. The March 2025 SAM.gov migration maintained reporting and public access routes.
- **High Risk:** Fiscal Service’s workforce plan explicitly implements Administration workforce directives. However, I did not establish an implemented Administration-directed restriction on USAspending’s published fields, coverage, or access, a negative policy disclaimer, or a presidential-action-driven spending-data ICR.
- **Gone:** No termination directive was found.

### Political context that should not be misattributed

DOGE’s spending claims made USAspending especially important to journalists and auditors. [NPR](https://text.npr.org/nx-s1-5302705) used downloaded USAspending records to check contract-savings claims; GAO did likewise.

[CBS reported removal of USAID contract details from DOGE’s “Wall of Receipts”](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doge-usaid-contracts-details-removed-wall-of-receipts/). **That was a different website—not evidence of removal from USAspending.gov.** Likewise, grant cancellations change underlying spending activity; they do not necessarily mean spending records have been suppressed.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

There are concrete proposed reporting changes, meeting the rubric’s pending-change criterion. Their apparent direction is largely greater disclosure, so this rating indicates **policy change and comparability risk**, not demonstrated censorship.

**Confidence: High that changes were proposed; Medium on their ultimate implementation.**

## Preservation implications

**Preserve now, but prioritize versioning over an emergency rescue of a demonstrably disappearing platform.**

The principal risks are losing reproducible historical states and receiving less complete or timely upstream records. Recommended actions:

- Capture dated award, transaction, account, and subaward extracts separately.
- Retain schemas, validation rules, rights notices, and submission-statistics snapshots.
- Monitor agency submission dates and missing-account indicators.
- Compare field coverage and reporting lag across successive snapshots.
- Reassess staffing when actual bureau headcounts and enacted funding become available.
- Track final action on OMB’s 2026 proposed rule.

No evidence found establishes that independent copies comprehensively preserve every USAspending product or prior version. Public downloads and open software make preservation feasible, but are not substitutes for an actual preservation program.
